newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices retreat as U.S. stocks rise.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices retreat as U.S. stocks rise.

text.p: World oil prices retreated to near their lowest for six months on Thursday after data showed rising crude stocks in the United States, the world's largest energy market, traders said.
Benchmark Brent April crude futures were trading down 42 cents a barrel at $20.21 in mid-afternoon, after touching a session low of $20.11, one cent above a six-month low touched on Tuesday.

American Petroleum Institute stock figures released after the market closed on Wednesday showed U.S. crude oil inventories rose by 3.12 million barrels last week, an expected rise in view of maintenance work at U.S. refineries.
Stock data from the U.S. Department of Energy's Energy Information Administration said crude stocks grew 4.4 million barrels, when traders were expecting a build of 3.275 million barrels.

"It is clear now that the tight fundamentals seen in all three major product markets during the fall is dissipating fast," Washington-based Petroleum Finance Company said in a market commentary, referring to the European, Pacific, Atlantic Basin markets.
"Global demand for crude has already begun to weaken in the Atlantic Basin with the start of refinery maintenance season in the United States" and poor financial returns from refining, it added.
Demand for heating oil, which provided support for higher prices earlier this year, has fallen steadily in the last few weeks as supplies were replenished and the weather became milder.
But some brokers drew encouragement from declines in U.S. product supplies, particularly gasoline, ahead of the driving season, and bullish short-term technicals.
Gasoline stocks fell by 1.3 million barrels and distillates by 2.9 million, the API said.
Prices had made up some ground on Wednesday, with dealers saying the limited recovery was hardly surprising given the 15 percent decline in prices since the end of January.
The private forecaster Weather Services Corp predicted well above normal temperatures in the Northeast U.S., the world's largest heating oil market, at least until Friday.
